belt: Hi — I'm ready to start Define on our project.

reply.answer:
Welcome — I'm here to coach you and your team through your improvement project step by step, so you don't need to be an expert. We'll work through five phases together:
• Define — pin down the problem and who's solving it
• Measure — get the real numbers
• Analyse — find the true root cause
• Improve — test and apply the fix
• Control — make the gains stick
Right now we're in Define — the most important phase, because a clear problem is half the solution. For each of the thirteen parts I'll explain what it is and why it matters, show you a finished example, then ask for yours. When all thirteen are agreed, you and your team review the Define report and approve it.

Let’s start with the **business case**. The business case says why this project deserves time and people: what is going wrong, where and since when, how big it is today, and what it costs. It is what earns the project its support. People outside the team only back what they can understand and size — and it is the first thing the Define report shows.
reply.explanation: The business case explains why the project deserves resources — what is wrong, where and since when, how big it is, and what it costs.
reply.example: During January to June 2026, 12% of invoices produced by UK billing were returned for correction, against 3% for the rest of the group. The rework and delayed payments cost about €35k a month.
reply.prompt: Why is your project worth doing? Tell me what is going wrong, where and since when, how big it is today, and roughly what it costs.

Next: the problem statement — this is where we define the pain clearly, so the team works on the same problem. It describes what is happening, where, since when, how much, and how you know, but names no cause and no solution. We use the 5W2H framework — What, Where, When, Who, Why, How, and How much — to structure this.

Why it matters: A clear problem definition is the heart of Define. It ensures everyone understands what the problem is and why it’s worth solving, without jumping ahead to causes or solutions.

Here’s an example to illustrate:

| Question | How it is formulated | Example |
|----------|-----------------------|---------|
| What     | the defect, in one noun phrase | invoices returned for correction |
| Where    | the process and place | UK billing, order to invoice |
| When     | the period, or since when | January to June 2026 |
| Who      | who is affected | client finance teams, credit control |
| Why      | why it matters to them | wrong amounts delay payment and trust |
| How      | how the defect shows up | clients return the invoice or dispute it |
| How much | the size, against a requirement | 12% of invoices, against 3% elsewhere |

Composed example: "From January to June 2026, 12% of invoices produced by UK billing were returned by clients for correction — four times the 3% seen elsewhere — delaying payment for client finance teams and credit control."

fields.label: voc summary
fields.value: Our customers are the suppliers, who need paying on the agreed 30-day terms, and our own ward managers, who need stock to keep arriving. Suppliers complain most about payments arriving late and not knowing when they will be paid; ward managers about deliveries being held. One more thing: suppliers also told us they cannot see the status of an invoice once it is submitted.

fields.label: problem statement
fields.value: From January to June 2026, 23% of supplier invoices handled by the accounts payable team across our three hospital sites were paid after their 30-day terms. Suppliers chased payments by phone and email, and some put us on stop, holding up ward stock. This caused interest charges, lost discounts, and supplier stops.

fields.label: baseline estimate
fields.value: One metric: late payment rate, in %, meaning the share of supplier invoices paid more than 30 days after the invoice date. It is about 23% today, from the AP ledger for January to June 2026. It feeds our finance KPI, creditor days.

value.in_scope: invoice receipt to payment release for purchase-order invoices at our three hospital sites.
value.out_scope: non-PO invoices, payroll, procurement tendering, and the ERP system itself.

fields.label: goal statement
fields.value: Reduce the late payment rate from 23% to under 5% by 31 March 2027, and keep it under 5% for three months after that.

fields.label: target value
fields.value: Late payment rate: under 5% of supplier invoices.

fields.label: target date
fields.value: We plan to finish the project by 31 March 2027 (2027-03-31).

value.cost_of_gap: About £68,000 a year in interest and lost discounts, from the savings calculation.
value.realisation_schedule: It would start in Q2 2027 at about £17,000 a quarter.
value.finance_contact: Sam Reid, management accountant, who will validate it.

fields.label: secondary metrics
fields.value: Two things must not get worse: the number of supplier payment queries the AP team handles each month, and AP staff overtime hours. Both should stay at or below today's levels.

value.suppliers: our medical and general suppliers, and the purchasing team who raise the purchase orders
value.inputs: supplier invoices, purchase orders and goods-received notes
value.process_steps: receive the invoice, match it to the purchase order and the goods receipt, resolve mismatches, approve, then schedule and release payment
value.customers: the suppliers, and our ward managers who rely on their deliveries
value.process_metrics: days from invoice receipt to payment release, and the share of invoices with a match exception

fields.label: issues and barriers
fields.value: Two barriers: the three sites use different approval routes, and an ERP change freeze until January limits system changes. One risk: AP staff turnover over the winter.
